subjective.question: What is the integumentary system? Describe the integument of protozoans and multicellular invertebrates. The integumentary system is the outer covering of the animal body (skin and its derivatives) that provides protection against mechanical injury, infection, desiccation and harmful radiation, and also helps in temperature regulation, excretion and sensation. In protozoans the body is covered only by a thin plasma membrane; in some forms a protective pellicle or a shell/test is present. In multicellular invertebrates the integument consists of a single-layered epidermis, often covered by a cuticle (as in annelids and arthropods); in arthropods the cuticle is hardened into a protective exoskeleton, and in molluscs the mantle secretes a calcareous shell.

Describe the structure of mammalian skin. Mammalian skin consists of two main layers. (1) Epidermis: the outer, stratified squamous epithelial layer; rapid cell division occurs in its deeper parts and the dead, keratinized cells at the surface are continuously shed. It bears derivatives such as hair, nails/claws and epidermal glands (sebaceous, sweat and mammary glands). (2) Dermis: the inner, thicker connective-tissue layer containing blood vessels, nerves, sensory receptors, hair follicles and glands. Below the dermis lies the hypodermis with fat deposits that insulate the body.

What are mineralized tissues? Which animals possess them? Mineralized tissues are body tissues hardened by the deposition of inorganic minerals, mainly calcium salts (calcium carbonate or calcium phosphate), e.g. bone, dentine, molluscan shell and the exoskeleton of many invertebrates. They provide support, protection and leverage for movement. About two-thirds of the living species that contain mineralized tissues are invertebrates, although the most complex mineralized skeletons are those of vertebrates.

Write a note on the scales of fishes. Fish scales are dermal in origin in bony fishes (teleosts), i.e. they develop from the dermis of the skin. Placoid scales of cartilaginous fishes (sharks) are tooth-like and have both epidermal and dermal contributions. Ganoid scales are found in primitive bony fishes, while cycloid and ctenoid scales are the thin, overlapping scales of modern teleosts. Scales protect the body, reduce friction during swimming and grow by the addition of new layers, producing growth rings.

What are feathers? Describe their functions in birds. Feathers are epidermal derivatives unique to birds, made of the protein keratin. They are important in (1) flying — flight feathers of wings and tail form the flight surface; (2) thermal regulation — down feathers trap air and insulate the body; (3) behaviour — coloured feathers are used in display, courtship and camouflage; and (4) protection of the skin from water and injury.

Compare hydrostatic skeleton, exoskeleton and endoskeleton. Organisms have 3 kinds of skeletons. (1) Hydrostatic skeleton: muscles act against an incompressible fluid-filled body cavity (earthworm, sea anemone); it is soft, flexible and suitable for burrowing and swimming in soft-bodied animals. (2) Exoskeleton: a hard external covering secreted by the epidermis (arthropods, molluscs) that protects and gives muscle-attachment sites but limits growth, so it is shed during moulting. (3) Endoskeleton: an internal framework of cartilage and/or bone (vertebrates) that grows with the body, supports large size and provides internal leverage for locomotion.

Histologically, what does cartilage consist of? How is it different from bone? Histologically, cartilage consists of three components: cells (chondrocytes lying in lacunae), fibres (collagen and elastic fibres) and a cellular (ground) matrix rich in chondrin. It is flexible, avascular and lacks nerves. Bone, in contrast, is a mineralized tissue whose mature cells are called osteocytes (bone cells); it is hard and rigid because of calcium salts, has a rich blood supply, and forms the endoskeleton of most vertebrates.

Describe the structure of a skeletal muscle fibre and the sarcomere. Each skeletal muscle is made of muscle fibres (cells), and each muscle fibre is surrounded by a membrane called the sarcolemma. Inside, the fibre contains many myofibrils, which are composed of myofilaments of two types: thick filaments of myosin and thin filaments of actin (with troponin and tropomyosin). The repeating unit of the myofibril is the sarcomere; an electron microscope reveals the precise placement of actin and myosin within the sarcomere, which gives skeletal muscle its striated appearance of alternating dark and light bands.

Explain the cross-bridge mechanism of muscle contraction. Skeletal muscle contracts only when stimulated by a motor neuron. On stimulation, Ca2+ is released and binds troponin, moving tropomyosin so that the binding sites on actin are exposed. The myosin head binds to actin, forming a cross bridge. The myosin head then bends (power stroke), pulling the thin filament toward the centre of the sarcomere, and ATP binding breaks the cross bridge so the cycle can repeat. In this way the sarcomere shortens without the filaments themselves changing length (sliding-filament model). The events regulating skeletal muscle contraction are electrical, chemical and molecular.

What are the physiological properties of muscle tissue? Muscle tissue shows three main physiological properties: (1) Excitability — the ability to respond to a stimulus (usually from a motor neuron); (2) Contractility — the ability to shorten forcibly and generate force; and (3) Extensibility — the ability to be stretched or extended beyond resting length. Smooth muscles are involuntary in action, whereas skeletal muscles are voluntary and cardiac muscle is involuntary but autorhythmic.

Describe non-muscular movement in animals. Many animals or cells move without muscles. (1) Amoeboid movement occurs by flowing of cytoplasm into pseudopodia, as in Amoeba and white blood cells. (2) Ciliary movement uses the coordinated beating of cilia; ciliary movements are well coordinated in protozoa such as Paramecium and also move materials over epithelia in multicellular animals. (3) Flagellar movement uses long whip-like flagella, e.g. in Euglena and sperm cells. In vertebrates, locomotion occurs by the combined association of the endoskeleton, skeletal muscles and tendons.

Write a note on the water vascular system of echinoderms. The water vascular system is a unique hydraulic system of canals and tube feet found in echinoderms such as the starfish. Water enters through the madreporite and circulates through the stone canal, ring canal and radial canals into the tube feet. By regulating water pressure, the animal extends and retracts the tube feet, which act as suction organs; in echinoderms this system is a unique means of locomotion, and it also helps in food capture and gas exchange.

Describe the structure of a neuron and the role of glial cells. A neuron consists of a cell body (containing the nucleus), dendrites that receive signals, and a long axon that conducts the nerve impulse to other cells; the giant axon of the squid is about one meter long and one mm in diameter, which made it a classic experimental material. Glial cells are the supporting cells of the nervous system: they supply nutrients and oxygen to neurons, maintain the chemical environment, form myelin (Schwann cells in the peripheral nervous system) and protect neurons from pathogens.

What is a reflex arc? Trace the path of a reflex action. The path of a reflex action is called the reflex arc. It consists of five components: (1) a receptor that detects the stimulus; (2) a sensory neuron carrying the impulse to the central nervous system; (3) an integration centre (interneuron) in the spinal cord or brain; (4) a motor neuron carrying the impulse out; and (5) an effector (muscle or gland) that produces the response. Reflexes are rapid, involuntary and protective responses that do not require conscious thought.

Describe the divisions of the nervous system. The central nervous system (CNS) includes both the brain and the spinal cord; the spinal cord contains grey matter, white matter and sensory/motor fibres, and is surrounded by three meninges — dura mater, arachnoid and pia mater. The peripheral nervous system consists of cranial and spinal nerves (in frog there are only ten pairs of spinal nerves). The autonomic nervous system divides into sympathetic and parasympathetic parts, which generally act antagonistically on visceral organs; the parasympathetic system emerges from the brain (cranial) and sacral regions.

Describe the main parts of the vertebrate brain. The vertebrate brain develops from the tubular nerve cord and has three main regions. (1) Forebrain: it has two main parts, the telencephalon (cerebrum, olfactory bulbs and limbic system) and the diencephalon (thalamus and hypothalamus); the cerebrum is the brain part larger in birds and mammals. (2) Midbrain: integrates visual and auditory signals. (3) Hindbrain: it includes the pons, cerebellum and medulla oblongata — all of them. The cerebellum coordinates balance and locomotor control and is much larger in birds and mammals, while the medulla oblongata, well developed in jawed vertebrates, contains reflex centres for breathing, swallowing and cardiovascular control.

How is the constant concentration of Na+ and K+ ions maintained across the nerve membrane? The constant concentration of Na+ and K+ ions on both sides of the membrane is maintained by the action of the Na+/K+ pump (sodium-potassium ATPase). Using energy from ATP, the pump actively transports three Na+ ions out of the cell for every two K+ ions pumped in. This maintains the resting membrane potential, with high K+ inside and high Na+ outside, which is essential for the conduction of nerve impulses.

Write a note on photoreceptors in invertebrates. Photoreceptors detect light. Simple photoreceptors include eyespots and ocelli — ocelli are common in arthropods, annelids and molluscs and can detect light intensity and direction but cannot form images. In earthworms, photoreceptors are scattered over the epidermis, allowing the animal to respond to light without true eyes. Compound eyes of arthropods are complex photoreceptors made of many ommatidia that form a mosaic image.

Describe the common defects of the vertebrate eye. (1) Nearsightedness (myopia): close objects are seen clearly but distant objects appear blurred, because the eyeball is too long and the image focuses in front of the retina. (2) Farsightedness (hyperopia): distant objects are clear but close objects are not focused properly, because the eyeball is too short. (3) Astigmatism: blurred vision due to the irregular shape of the cornea or the curvature of the lens. (4) Cataract: the inner lens becomes darkened or opaque. (5) Glaucoma: damage to the optic nerve, usually from raised intraocular pressure, which can result in vision loss and blindness. The size of the human eye ball is about 24 mm in diameter.

What is the tapetum lucidum? Explain eye shine in animals. The tapetum lucidum is a layer of tissue in the eye of many vertebrates lying immediately behind the retina. It functions as a retroreflector, reflecting visible light back through the retina and increasing the light available to the photoreceptors, thus improving night vision. When light shines into the eye of an animal having a tapetum, the pupil appears to glow — this is eye shine, a type of iridescence seen in many animals in colours such as white, blue, green, yellow, pink and red.

Describe the structure and working of the vertebrate ear. The ear has three parts. The outer ear collects sound waves and directs them to the tympanic membrane (ear drum); the Eustachian (auditory) tube equalizes air pressure between the middle ear and the throat. The middle ear contains three ossicles — malleus, incus and stapes; the malleus adheres to the tympanic membrane and connects to the incus, and the ossicles amplify the vibrations to the oval window. In the inner ear, the cochlea converts vibrations into nerve impulses, while the vestibular apparatus (semicircular canals) is responsible for equilibrium; the vestibular nerve carries balance signals to the brain.

Write a note on the lateral line system and electroreception in fishes. Fishes have a lateral line system in the body: a series of canals and neuromast receptors under the skin that detect vibrations, water currents and the movements of other animals, helping in orientation and schooling. In addition, the ampullary organs (ampullae of Lorenzini) in fishes can sense the feeble electrical fields produced by organisms living in the surrounding water, enabling the fish to locate hidden prey.

How do snakes sample airborne chemicals? Also explain olfaction. The sense of smell is called olfaction, and nasal sensation is interpreted by the olfactory nerve, which contains information related to smell. Snakes use their protrusible, forked tongue to take samples of airborne chemicals: the tongue flicks out, picks up odour molecules and delivers them to the Jacobson's (vomeronasal) organ in the roof of the mouth, which analyses the chemical signals and helps the snake track prey and mates.

Write short notes on any three types of invertebrate receptors. (1) Tactile receptors respond to touch and mechanical contact — web-building spiders have tactile receptors to sense prey struggling in their webs, and annelids bear tactile receptors that allow them to retract quickly into their tubes. (2) Hygroreceptors detect humidity; in insects they are identified on the antennae, palps and near the spiracles. (3) Baroreceptors respond to pressure changes. (4) Thermoreceptors sense thermal variations, and phonoreceptors such as the tympanal organs of crickets and grasshoppers detect sound. Invertebrates possess all of these categories of sensory receptors.
